text: I will model the **fluid volume**, not the metal. I interpret the axial inlet as the open impeller eye: an annulus from the 12 mm hub radius to the 16 mm blade-leading-edge radius in the shroud plane. The passage is 14 mm high above the backplate, bounded radially at 58 mm. Seven blades follow a smooth 30° backward sweep from radius 16 to 58 mm. I will first make an intentionally coarse conformal volume mesh (target size about 2 mm), so I will omit the requested 2 mm root fillets at this stage because they are only one cell radius and would not be resolved reliably. I’ll construct and inspect the CAD fluid volume first.

The installed CAD API supports direct algebraic faces and extrusions. I’ll now create one blade from two sampled offset curves, pattern it seven times, subtract the blades and hub from a closed annular passage, and print the requested geometric measurements before rendering the coarse CAD.

The previous probe only failed because one queried convenience constructor is absent; it made no geometry. I’ll use the supported `Face(Wire.make_polygon(...))` construction directly and keep every design parameter explicit in metres.

The coarse CAD is one connected fluid volume with the correct principal dimensions. I’ll now view it from above and obliquely, including the open annular eye and the seven swept passage boundaries, before assigning any patches or meshing it.

The preview confirms the intended annular eye and overall passage envelope; the dense black lines are tessellation edges on the horizontal passage faces, not extra blades. I’ll inspect the exact CAD faces by orientation and radius so patch assignment is based on the faces themselves rather than bounding-box position guesses.

Face inspection caught a real defect: the patterned blade compound was not subtracted as seven solids, so the preview’s lines were indeed only tessellation. I will correct the boolean by subtracting each blade sequentially and verify the removed volume and resulting blade-wall faces before proceeding.

The seven blade solids exist but still report zero intersection with the annulus, so this is now clearly a placement/coordinate issue rather than a boolean-compound issue. I’ll inspect both bounding boxes and one intersection directly.

The blade footprint’s wire orientation caused a signed extrusion downward; translating it by 4 mm left it below the passage. I’ll force the extrusion vector upward explicitly, rebuild all seven cutters, and replace `fluid` with the corrected result.
This API requires both a positive amount and a direction selector. I’ll repeat the corrected construction with both supplied; the failed cell altered no final geometry.

The corrected boolean removes 13.623 cm³ of blade volume and leaves one connected water region. The sampled curve creates many planar blade-side facets, which is geometrically accurate but unnecessarily fragmented. Before deciding whether to smooth that representation, I’ll inspect face-type counts and re-render the actually cut volume.

The corrected view shows seven open backward-curved passages, an annular axial eye, and seven radial exits. I’ll retain the faceted CAD blade curves because their maximum chord error is tiny relative to the 2 mm coarse cells, while they make patch identity unambiguous. Next I’ll assign exact CAD faces: horizontal bottom → backplate; horizontal top inside 16 mm → inlet; remaining top → shroud; radius-12 cylinders → hub; radius-58 cylinders → outlet; every other vertical face → blades. Then I’ll export all patches in one welded tessellation.
I’ll first count the proposed groups and print their total areas as a sanity check. This will catch, for example, a blade wall accidentally mistaken for an outlet segment before tessellation.

You’re right. The only unresolved issue is splitting the single coplanar top CAD face at the 16 mm eye radius. I’ll do that as a conformal partition inside Gmsh, put both resulting volumes in one fluid physical region so their shared faces become internal, generate a coarse tetrahedral mesh immediately, and convert it to OpenFOAM.

The mesher finished successfully (30,348 nodes, 173,404 total elements); conversion alone failed because an otherwise empty case lacked `system/controlDict`. I’ll add the minimal mesh-only case dictionary, convert the already-written mesh, and run the binding mesh check now.
I’ll re-emit the conversion/check cell with its own `subprocess` import so it is reproducible in `build.py`, and print the actual error tail rather than only standard output.

Conversion created the volume and three curved/vertical patches; Gmsh left the coplanar top and bottom faces in `defaultFaces`. I’ll add the two dictionaries `checkMesh` requires, then verify topology before splitting that default patch geometrically into inlet, shroud, and backplate.

The coarse mesh is valid: 131,178 tetrahedra, one connected region, closed boundary, and `Mesh OK`. I’ll now split only the horizontal `defaultFaces` by boundary-face centers: annular eye at the top → inlet, remaining top → shroud, bottom → backplate. Then I’ll rename any residual default patch only if empty and re-check.

`setToFace` is not available in this OpenFOAM build. I’ll avoid set copying: create the shroud set directly from the top box, then delete the inlet cylinder from that same set using the supported `cylinderToFace` source.

The requested horizontal patches now exist (124 inlet faces, 13,260 shroud faces, 13,388 backplate faces). I’ll run `checkMesh` again and inspect the final boundary table; any nonempty residual `defaultFaces` must be identified rather than silently accepted.

The final mesh has exactly six nonempty boundary patches and no residual default patch; the `".*"` line in `checkMesh` is OpenFOAM’s aggregate regex entry, not a seventh patch. `checkMesh` passes with one region. I’ll now export the mesh to VTK and render the surface plus a cutaway/cell view to visually confirm the passages are actually meshed.

The VTK export confirms all six patches are independently readable. I’ll render them with distinct colors and overlay the tetrahedral edges in a clipped half-domain, then remove the bulky temporary VTK directory while retaining the PNG.

The visual check confirms the water passages, annular inlet, seven radial exits, and all six named patches. I’ll record the modeling assumption and fillet omission in the case, run one final binding `checkMesh`, and print final mesh/patch statistics.

The final mesh passes the binding check. It contains 131,178 tetrahedra in one connected region and all six requested boundary patches. The only intentionally unmodeled feature is the 2 mm root fillet, omitted because it is below the coarse mesh’s 2.5–4 mm target size.
